utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, General. The affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies, and Mr. Djurdjic is near the end of his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Well, the end is in sight, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few more documents for us to go through so may we have Defence Exhibit D003-2555 next, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see this document. It hasn't got the stamp, I don't know why. There's just a handwritten entry, but that's not contentious; I know that the judiciary and the court's function during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is a document about mobilisation, mobilised courts, and military prosecutors and so on. And I'd like to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned D00199, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document, please, is exhibit under 65 ter 1918.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It just shows us that the Supreme Command staff throughout the war took account of the judiciary and military courts and the importance that it attached to them; do you agree with that, that that is the gist of this document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00200, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next exhibit is D003-2753, a Defence document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the same thing again. I'm familiar with this kind of format and this kind of document once again relating to the military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned D00201, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is D003-2736.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we zoom in if you want me to read through the document to see what it actually says, please. Yes, here we have the priorities set out in conducting criminal proceedings, and I can see that the date is the 8th of June, which is almost the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned D00202, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The next document is D003-2999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, am I right in saying that this is a document from the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia dated the 18th of April, 1992 [sic]. It is in fact an order, and the application of Article 17 of the Law on Defence and Subordination pursuant to that, or resubordination?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned D00203, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At line 14, I suspect the year is 1999, although we can see that from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, the transcript wrongly has 1992. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think we need to correct that, do we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see the document is dated -- it appears as though it could be 1992, and yet I suspect it's a 9, 1999, that is underlined. That may be the source of the mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's a document dated the 18th of April, 1999. And then we have other documents, one we saw by the chief of the Supreme Command, and I'm now going to propose to put forth two more documents which are a set and follow on from this order on subordination. So I hope the usher won't mind if I've got the number wrong, 65 ter document, 1722 is the number according to my records, but I might have got that wrong, so I apologise if I have. And it is not exhibited yet. It's an order by the commander of the 3rd Army dated the 20th of April, 1999. Yes, it has been admitted. I'm told it has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Do you want me to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Well, I'd like to tender this document now. The next document under 65 ter is 1504 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. These documents are of varying importance and those that are more important we are trying to absorb as we go, Mr. Djurdjic. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document under 65 ter 01722 will be assigned D00204.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document under 65 ter is 1504, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is a whole series of documents relating to resubordination of the MUP organs, and this is at the level of the Pristina Corps, assignment to the brigades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you tender that, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be assigned D00205, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The next document I'd like called up under 65 ter is 2809.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, this is another order of the Pristina Corps dated the 25th of April. Do you agree that by this order the Pristina Corps in fact sets out in greater detail the order that was issued previously of the 3rd Army of the 20th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And what is regulated here in point 4 is that the military conscripts which had thus far been temporarily engaged in the MUP reserve units be returned to their original war units, and that is set out in point 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you look at para 1, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In para 1 or point 1, it says that these units should remain Special Police units, and the territorial units of MUP, that is to say the OPG and others, the detachments, which were locally positioned. They remained within the composition and under the authority of the MUP forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, no, read point 1.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Engage forces of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, PJP Special Police forces, manoeuvre detachments, and MUP territorial units to carry out combat tasks in the PRK zone. In the zone of the Pristina Corps -- let me repeat, engage the units of the MUP of Serbia and then: Manoeuvre detachments, Special Police units, and MUP territorial units. Other forces and institutions shall continue to remain under the jurisdiction of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. So these units are being resubordinated and still remain under the army and outside that composition they come under the jurisdiction of MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. That means that these units, the PJP units and the manoeuvre detachments and territorial units are resubordinated whereas other organisational units continue to perform their tasks under the jurisdiction of the ministry of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this is in conformity with the principles of resubordination, the forces are resubordinated for combat whereas -- and these are units carrying out combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When it comes to combat operations, would you agree with me when I say that during the war in 1999, this resubordination was carried out at the level of the brigades, and that it was the brigades who were the protagonists of the combat action, who engaged in combat action?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, because the brigades were tactical units, that is, the lowest level or rather highest level of tactical units. Not the lowest, I meant to say highest. The highest tactical unit which in fact organises and carries out complex combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you agree with me when I say that not a single corps operation that is operation of the Pristina Corps during the war was carried out?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what, I can't say that because the corps is given the task and assignment from the army command; and all corps units, therefore, objectively speaking, are deployed and engaged. And if you look at the orders from the corps command, for instance, in point 4 where the decision is made as to the manner in which the corps will be deployed and engaged, later on through point 5 all the corps units, almost all of them are given combat assignments. Now, whether that is in fact a corps operation, I would say that all the forces of the corps, the combat forces of the corps, were engaged for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll go into that subject with somebody else then. The corps operations during the war didn't exist, they were all at the level of the brigade. But let's move on, I'll take that up with someone else.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, am I right in saying that the MUP and its organs were not the subject of operative processing of the security administration?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as we've come to the war, let me say -- ask you this: Pursuant to the Law on Defence, it is the duty of all state organs including the MUP to compile a war plan?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did the MUP too have to, in view of the situation that existed at the beginning of 1999 and at the end of 1998, have to take measures in conformity with its war plan and pursuant to its war plan?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only in conformity with the war plan, but also in conformity with the situation on the ground. Because a war plan is devised and made up for an assumed situation in the future which emanates from an estimation that that situation would come about. So that -- and those documents are termed the state secret. And then the plan is updated. Now, MUP action is commensurate to the situation on the ground which can be outside what has been planned in a war plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know if you know that within the Ministry of the Interior there was a department charged with war preparations?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That department closely cooperated with the corresponding services of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As well as with all other organs of the Ministry of Defence and the various companies which were supposed to have their own war plans devised. Some institutions and companies had to have developed their own war plans in keeping with the orders of the level of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: As regards the department of the MUP, accordingly all army units had similar war plans because there was a need to act in a harmonised way when implementing all those war plans?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was envisaged that even lower-ranking units have their own war plans in keeping with the general war plan of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that according to the war plans there was a possibility envisaged that various commands and other state organs and institutions be transferred to another location?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the activities was deployment or movement to the war locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In the army, it is the main command post, a forward command post, and as for civilian organs it -- they had their own locations?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not only command posts, but also material supplies which would then be transferred from peacetime locations to wartime locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that the Ministry of the Interior relocated from Knez Milos Street 103 at the beginning of the war when the state of war was declared?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that by that time everyone had relocated and that most of those buildings were empty at the time when targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that the ministers and chiefs of services were relocated to various locations around Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where they relocated, but since their buildings were empty, they must have had their war locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the ministry by virtue of its activity, which covered the entire territory of Serbia, still directed operations from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where they directed operations from.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see the minister, Vlajko Stojiljkovic, during the war?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear that the ministry or rather certain of its parts were in different locations, one of those being the commercial bank in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I only know for the location of the state security service that was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are overlapping and not pausing, they'll have to repeat the last two questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We'll have to repeat. Can you tell me where was the state security service relocated?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we attended a meeting during the war to see Mr. Rade Markovic, we went to the general area of Dedinje towards the highway and greenhouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Given the nature of your work, you were familiar in terms of cooperation with the state security sector rather than the public security sector given the different remits of the two sectors?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our basic tasks coincided more with the tasks of the state security service than the public security service. In any case, we cooperated with both of them if there were such problems that required cooperation with the public security sector, although it did not happen as frequently as with the state security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I looked through some documents and it seems to me that you cooperated mostly with the state security in bringing in conscripts which -- who fled their units or were supposed to report to their units; therefore, the police had most work in that regard?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for us to meet in particular with the republican sector of public security because the number of such people was not so great. Our manning strength was almost always up to 100 per cent. In any case, this would have been one of the regular tasks which would require our communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that throughout the war, the public security sector performed their legally prescribed security related tasks such as keeping public law and order, detecting and prosecuting crimes and defenders, as well as traffic control, border control, fire-fighting, and administrative tasks?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Since there was a state of war, did you know that in the entire territory of the Republic of Serbia their main task was to secure persons in certain locations that were targeted?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and also should there have been a location that was bombed, they were in charge of on-site investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And the other tasks I mentioned such as fire-fighting, those were all tasks of the public security sector?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and they were quite successful in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the police had to be informed of all locations that were bombed in order for them to draft reports, and that was one of the main tasks of the public security sector throughout Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask -- well, not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, are you familiar in detail with the functioning and organisation of the Ministry of the Interior, or does your knowledge come as a result of your long career and the tasks you worked on?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the ministry in general, not in a detailed fashion, since there was no need for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You must know, I believe, that the minister prescribes the way minister tasks are to be implemented and he also provides instructions on how to do so?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think any minister does that within their own respective ministries.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Certain details you mentioned such as decisions on the formation of the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit as well as PJP police units comes from your general knowledge rather than from you seeing those specific documents during the war?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see such documents, but I do know that such units existed, and I'm familiar with their basic tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you probably don't know who it was that could order the assembly and deployment of such units and in what way, are you familiar with such details?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assembly of such units, as far as I know, was done in 1998 due to the situation in Kosovo, and they were sent there in shifts. This concerns the PJP units. They rotated. I don't know, though, whether their shifts lasted for a fortnight or three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You now said that these units rotated, who was it that could make a decision about that, are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not. I suppose that was regulated by virtue of the orders of the minister of the interior and tasks were assigned pursuant to what had been decided on the sessions of the Supreme Defence Council, or the sessions of another body.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have document P57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you mean to tender the last document we studied?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I thought we have dealt with that document some time ago, but obviously I'm not focused enough today. I would kindly seek to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document under 65 ter 02809, Your Honours, will be assigned D00206.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it, and I see the names of the persons tasked with specific tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the person in charge of this staff for the suppression of terrorism was Sreten Lukic in June 1998?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And deputy head of the staff, do you know that it was David Gajic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him, but I didn't know he was the deputy head of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where did David Gajic work?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the state security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In addition to being a member of the staff, do you know whether he held any other positions in Kosova-Metohija in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in charge of the state security sector in Kosova-Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The fourth name, can you tell us who that is, assistant head for special operations?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Milorad Lukovic, aka Legija, who otherwise commanded the JSO units of the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: State security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to page 2 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: At the end of the list, can you have a look at that portion of the document and tell us who were the additional members of the staff?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way it is written it included chiefs of the Secretariats for Internal Affairs and centres and branches of the RDB in Kosova-Metohija. On request of the head of the person in charge of the staff, other employees of the ministry may be appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In item 2 we see the task of the staff. Do you agree with me that it was to plan, organise, and control the work and engagement of organisational units of the ministry; and also sent and detached units in suppressing terrorists in the autonomous province of Kosova-Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you comment item 3 for me, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Doesn't the witness indicate that he doesn't know about the organisation of the MUP in terms of his management? He just has a general knowledge of it. If he is shown a document like this and ask a question like that, he is of necessity speculating, he's being asked to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I believe what he is being asked to do is merely repeat what the document says, which is not of great value to us. He is not inputting his own knowledge. This is the way I understand the evidence. Continue, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have read it, and I see that this head of the staff was answerable to the minister concerning his actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Does this correspond to what you know, what you knew about the staff in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in part. I'm reading this with some attention because all the details are included. It's a shame if the commander of the Pristina Corps was not acquainted with this document because they had joint meetings. I see this document for the first time. Given my position, there was no need for me to see it earlier. However, I find it interesting to see who the persons involved were, some of whom I do know and, well, others I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Between 1999 and today during which period you gave statements on the functioning of the MUP and you provided your opinion, you did not know about this document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, after you were re-activated in service, did you attend meetings of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were re-activated, did you attend the collegium meetings of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war I did not, and after the war I think I did on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From the moment when you were re-activated, did you attend, occasionally, government meetings, meetings of the government of Yugoslavia or the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You will correct me if I'm mistaken, but I believe that from March up until the end of the war, you saw -- you went to see the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on three occasions, President Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see him three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I correct that you were not present when reports were submitted to the supreme commander and president of the FRY, Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not present, and I do not know who reported to him, who submitted the reports to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you attend the briefings at the office of the president of the Republic of Serbia, Milan Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never even saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you attend the briefings at the office of the president of the federal government, Momir Pjeletovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you attend briefings at the office of the president of the government of the Republic of Serbia, Mirko Marjanovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know that the federal minister of the interior was Mr. Zoran Sokolovic during the war and before the war?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the deputy minister -- the deputy federal minister of the interior was General Mile Puzovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know what his position was, but I did know that he held a responsible duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of what you knew about the state security sector in the course of your work, you told us over the past days that Jovica Stanisic requested when he was -- when Vlajko Stojiljkovic was appointed minister, that he brief the minister directly, that he report to the minister directly. Did I understand this correctly?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And am I right in saying that at that time when the president of Republic of Serbia was -- am I correct that the president of the Republic of Serbia at that time was Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, at that time he was the president of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, could I please -- could we please have document 3203 pulled up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the counsel please repeat the document number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D003-3203.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were we notified of this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that Ms. O'Leary did do this, that she supplemented our list, and I would appreciate it -- let me check if we have it. That's ERN number K022-7740. But, Your Honour, I believe there is an error in the transcript, an error in the formulation of my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: My question was, did I understand correctly that you said that Jovica Stanisic when he was -- when Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic was appointed as minister, that he did not report to him and brief him? And the witness said?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far -- as far as the information that I'm aware of is concerned, I can't say that this was done at the moment when he was appointed, when Vlajko Stojiljkovic was appointed minister. Rather when he -- during the time when he was minister and when he asked for Jovica Stanisic to brief him, he refused to do so and he requested that he be seen by President Milosevic. And I can say this man is no longer living, he died a while back so we can't really check on this, but that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you told me then that at the time the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was Slobodan Milosevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did look at this document, this was the period April 1997 and the signature there is of the President of Serbia Slobodan Milosevic. However, it isn't clear what kind of guide-lines are mentioned here. The sector of state security will conduct its operations in keeping with the guide-lines of the president of the Republic of Serbia, but I don't know what these guide-lines are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Since we do not have the translation of this, would you please read this decision from the start, starting with "state secret" please read it so that it's clear.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes: "Pursuant to Article 83 of the constitution of the Republic of Serbia, I hereby issue the following decision: First, at the time when preparations are made to adopt the federal law on security of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the sector of state security will conduct its operations in keeping with the guide-lines of the president of the republic and the government of the Republic of Serbia from the moment when this decision comes into force up until the day when the federal law is adopted, which in keeping with the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia provides that the tasks of security will be set forth in keeping with the jurisdiction of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. 2, this decision shall come into effect on the day of its adoption." And then the signature is the president of the republic, Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the year when this was adopted?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that, it was adopted on the 21st of April, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you to repeat this because what I heard as a translation was 1977, that's why I wanted you to repeated the year. Witness, at the time when this decision was adopted, do you agree that the president of Serbia was Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And that relates to the the portion of your testimony where you said that the chief of the sector was to report or brief him?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was like this: Both during the time of Rade Markovic and all other ministers, the sector of security, of state security, was within the Ministry of the Interior. That was how it was legally regulated. But as for in practice, practically the greatest influence over its work and the influence that was exerted on this person was -- or came from the relationship between the president of the Republic of Serbia, and the chief of the state security. And I can go back to 1997, the year when I came into this service. Regardless of how this was regulated by law, this man was directly connected or directly related to and briefed the president of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's what I was going to ask you about. Now, do you know what the constitutional provisions are of the authority of the president of the Republic of Serbia under the constitution of the Republic of Serbia of 1991, and what his competencies are in the area of state security?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the constitution provides.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let me ask you this: Did you know that at this time Mr. Rade Markovic was assistant minister of the interior? So I'm talking about 1977.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean 1997?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose assistant was he?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Assistant minister of the interior, and I think for crime, for general crime.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know he was in the public security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to ask you about this --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document into evidence with an MFI indication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, it won't be received; it will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be assigned D00207 MFI, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And while we are dealing with that, the document that you showed to the witness before this one, the decision to establish the ministerial staff for the suppression of terrorism, for the record it should be noted that is in fact Exhibit P57. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please pull up 65 ter document 5231. Can we please pull it up on the screens. I apologise, the number should be -- of this document should be 5231.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, as far as you know, when was the change at the head of the sector of state security carried out?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early October 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see here a decision to set up a collegium of the minister of the interior, and I refer you to items 2 and 3. Could you tell us who the members of this collegium were?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us the names for the record?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since this document is going to be admitted, I can read the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, just tell us the names.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radomir Markovic and his assistant Nikola Curcic -- his deputy, Nikola Curcic

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So at the time when this document was issued, Radomir Markovic was the assistant minister chief of the state security and Nikola Curcic was the deputy chief of the state security department; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And they were members of the collegium of the Minister of the Interior Vlajko Stojiljkovic; is that different compared to the period when Jovica Stanisic was at the head of the sector?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know; but I assume there was no difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, before this decision was issued, the chief of the department or the sector did not attend the meetings of the collegium of the minister of the interior, whereas here we see that those meetings were attended also by the chief and the deputy chief of the state security sector?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it was done during the period before this collegium, but I know that the sector of the interior, the sector of security, was a sector and not a service. And I said in general terms speaking that there were two sectors within the Ministry of the Interior: the state security and the public security sectors. So it would be logical that throughout the service one of the members of the collegium should also be the chief of the state security because he belongs to the Ministry of the Interior, and I assumed that that was the case before 1998, that it was the case in 1991 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, let's move on. Your assumption is wrong, and that's why I wanted to point this document out to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, you keep stating facts. You are not giving evidence. You must only ask questions of the witness. You don't tell him your assumption is wrong. I'm sure you understand the basic rules in that regard. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I did not mean to pursue this. I was going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, in your testimony so far you did not have in mind this document that I just pointed out to you, but you told us about the organisation of the Ministry of the Interior and what kind of relationships within it existed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know of this document, but I did not speak about the details. I always said that I knew what the organisation and structure was in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document is a 65 ter document, but it -- in its original form -- in its original form, this document is a two-page document and then there are some attachments which I have no idea how were forwarded to the OTP. So my proposal is that the first two pages of this document be adopted -- admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The whole document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that, Your Honours, will be assigned D00208.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps the second page can be brought onto the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've seen the entire document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like now to move on to another area. When you were in control from the 1st to the 7th of June in the Pristina Corps, I assume, and the 3rd Army, you talked to Sergej Perovic. Am I right in saying that he provided you with the initial information and that he said that that information should be verified?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, what part of his briefing and reporting?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I mean in Djakovica when he told you about the OPG.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that wasn't the initial information that I received and whether they should be verified and enhanced. Before that, I came to take over reports that were compiled by the security organs; and I received all these reports in great detail. And later on, the chief of the security sector of the 3rd Army compiled a summary. Now, what Sergej put forward, and relating to information on the ground where his brigade was located and so on, that was what he knew at the time; and there was no need to go into them in depth or to verify them. They were just received as a byproduct if I can use that term, as a byproduct to what he learned in relation to his regular work. So I didn't need to check it out nor was I in a position to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Well, I don't know if we need -- but let's look at the next document, and it is D003-2879, page 21083, lines 22 to 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, it's part of the statement made by Sergej Perovic, his testimony, in connection with what he was informing you about in Djakovica. And his answer when asked was: "I was given the assignment to check the veracity of those allegations, which I did. I spent a few days trying to establish the possible truth of this allegation; and after that, I informed Colonel Stojanovic that I was unable to confirm these allegations."

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And who gave him the assignment to check it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, when you were with him there and talked to him, he says that he checked it all out and that he informed Colonel Stojanovic with respect to that verification conducted by him. Perhaps Stojanovic gave him this task of assignment, but anyway it was with respect to what he reported to you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't give him any assignment to check this out. I don't know whether he received an assignment later on from someone and whether he acted upon it or not. I just told you what he reported to me, and that this was as I say, a byproduct of general information, that it wasn't my duty to check it out or take it any further than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony over the past few days --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, may I make myself clearer. If somebody needed to check this out then what they should have done was the chief of the security of the Pristina Corps should send a letter to the staff of the MUP of Kosovo and say, According to our additional information, we have received information that such and such had happened; please inform us whether this is reliable information or not. So that is now this should have been done. I don't see how else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've just remind me of something else, the document of the 25th of May, 1999, Pavkovic's, you've just reminded me of that. Do you happen to remember that General Pavkovic and General Lukic on the 4th of May submitted a report to the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and that a statement was issued to that effect about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I said that I was in Montenegro on the 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. Then we can move on. Yesterday, you mentioned -- well, I think you said that a politician from the SPS was Vlatkovic, can I remind you and tell you that there was a politician called Matkovic and that he was the minister for industry in the government of the Republic of Serbia and the director of a company at that time.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That he was in charge of developmental issues, the development of the economy in Kosovo and Metohija, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he was in charge of, but I do know that he was an official --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And a minister of the government of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why minister? Minister for what?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Minister of industry.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At line 24 of the last page, I heard words after the word "official," and I think it might be corrected later. I think for the purpose of today's proceedings, we should know what the witness said there. He said I know he was an official, and I heard the interpreters say something, but it's not recorded here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you going to have that confirmed with the witness, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. Let me see what it is, what you want me to do. I'm not clear on what I need to do. Line, what did you say the line was?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In line 24 we have an official, but I know that he was an official, what did you say, Witness? An official of what? Did you say he had a high-ranking position or what?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, I don't know what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: With respect to Matkovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me whether I knew that in the government of Serbia there was a Mr. Matkovic, and I said that yes I did know that; I was aware of that. So it's not Vlatkovic, it's Matkovic. I said Vlatkovic, but it's with an M, Matkovic. So you asked me whether it might have been Matkovic, and I said, Yes. And was he in the government of Serbia, and the director of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the name of what he was director of. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told me he was the minister of industry, I didn't know about that. But as I don't know English, I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly request that the witness repeat what the man was director of. Sartid, it sounded like S-a-r-t-i-d.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was director of Sartid. S-a-r-t-i-d.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a company in Smederevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's got to the bottom of that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, I'll move to the 8th of May, 1999, when Lieutenant-Colonel Djurovic came to see you. The reason why he came was the group of volunteers that entered Kosovo and Metohija circumventing the regular procedure. It was the Petrusic family, I believe that was why he came to see you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: On that occasion he informed you about Podujevo and mentioned the Skorpions and the crime that took place there. Did you know at the time that that group immediately following the incident was returned from Podujevo to Prolom Banja in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were returned, he didn't tell me anything about that. General Pavkovic found that group in Prolom Banja, and I have already discussed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said that you issued an order to the counter-intelligence group from Novi Sad to run checks. I suppose that was because you had heard those people originally came from Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to see the 65 ter document 4047.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I see the rest of the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I think this is the end of the page. The only thing at the bottom is security administration.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this document at all. There are also some incorrect facts. For example, if I see correctly, that they were in Bubanj Potok. They were issued uniforms in Bubanj Potok. No, no. As General Pavkovic reported, they were in NATO uniform with SAJ insignia. They could not have been in Bubanj Potok because at that time the reception centre, if that is what is alluded to, was already in Grocka. This is a highly suspicious document. I don't know of this document in security administration. It is the 13th of May. Then the 13th of May is security day and no one is in the office that day. We all attend ceremonies. I'm quite doubtful as to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But this document does have a ledger number?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This comes from the Supreme Command staff and security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I know, but this document is on the list of the Prosecution. We received it from them.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whose it is. In any case, it never says "security administration" at the bottom page. You always have the signature be it of the head or deputy head of administration. How they could have been issued with uniforms in the collection centre for volunteers? First of all, we didn't have any NATO uniforms and General Pavkovic saw them immediately upon his arrival in Prolom Banja and they were sporting those uniforms and I informed Sainovic accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where did you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went through the barricade in Bubanj Potok and on the 28th of March reached Prolom Banja. They were there awaited by Boca.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No military facility is mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but we all know that there was mention of the volunteer reception centre in Bubanj Potok. It says also they were issued with uniforms; they could not have received those at the barricade. The Bubanj Potok location is a toll booth on the highway. And at Bubanj Potok there was there was a barracks which housed the volunteer reception centre; but soon after it was targeted and destroyed, the centre was moved to Grocka. And that's where I was, after being re-activated. After being re-activated on the 27th of April, by that time that centre had been moved to Grocka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We have witness testimony as to how things developed, but there is no mention of the Bubanj Potok facility in the document. In any case, let's move on, there is a mention of 100 volunteers from Becej and Sid; do you see it in the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not an issue. Some information was checked pursuant to the document of the 12th of May. And Milan Milanovic, aka Mrgud, is mentioned. But in our document there is also mention made of Dalibor Novakovic, whom I don't see here. So some facts do tally, others do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this group went to Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say so in relation to this document. I testified to information received via Djurovic and what I learned from the intelligence group in Novi Sad. I also said that there were between 120 and 150 people involved, that there were two groups, one of which was formed by Mrgud and so on and so forth. They also returned two or three days before the report was drafted. They returned from Kosovo in early May according to that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the group that was Podujevo within SAJ had nothing to do with the group of Zivan Chetnik and the other group that was assembled by Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, I can't say anything. That group was assembled subsequently. In our report, it was stated that they were gathering again to leave for Kosovo and then General Ojdanic told us that that group should be prevented from reaching Kosovo at any cost. That group was formed subsequently. Vice-President Sainovic said so when he said that the SAJ seemed to have their own habits in assembling volunteers, and Rade Markovic said that they were a necessary evil in any war. I don't know what is in dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Concerning the two groups, I wanted to cite you in the Milutinovic case, if I can quickly find that, concerning the Hadzic group.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zivan Chetnik was behind the Hadzic group, I believe; right? Zivan Sokolovacki, aka Chetnik. Goran Hadzic was behind that group, and that group was supposed to go to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't seem to be able to find it. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you know that in 1991 in Slavonia in order to secure the oil rigs of the oil industry company of Krajina, a unit was formed tasked with providing security of that company?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that in 1991. Only when we ran checks on the Skorpions unit did we learn something about that. There were also articles in the weekly Vreme that dealt with it. In any case, in 1991 I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you they that the Vukovar Brigade in 1991 up to 1996 used that unit as necessary as a reserve force of the Army of Republika Srpska? No, not Republika Srpska but the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which Vukovar Brigade? What brigade is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The Army of the Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in 1996 when UNPROFOR took over Slavonia, Baranja, and western Serbia, the unit was disbanded handing over its weapons and equipment?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you I don't know about the Vukovar Brigade and what took place in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you know whether the unit was disbanded, the security unit, handing over their weapons and equipment?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have -- well, I first want to seek to tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness says A, he doesn't know it; B, he's doubtful to its authenticity, as I understand his evidence. You can have it marked for identification, but I don't think there's a secure enough foundation for it to be received in evidence at the moment. It will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be assigned D00210 MFI, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think I have already mentioned that this document was received from the Prosecution. We merely made use of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, am I right in saying that only after the war, perhaps in 2000 or 2001, it was learned for the first time that this unit may have committed crimes before 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the 17th of May, we briefed President Milosevic, as I've explained. The procedure was initiated by Natasa Kandic or the issue was raised by her, and then a trial ensued in Prokuplje. Some of them were -- some of them were provisionally released and issuing threats to the president of the court in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You did not understand my question. I'm not talking about Podujevo. Only after the war, after 1999, it was learned that they may have committed crimes prior to 1999.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I know that there were subjects of some articles of the weekly Vreme, but I don't know when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That was after the end of the war in 1999.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even before that, the Vreme wrote on paramilitary formations and I believe they were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In 1999, did you have any information?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can we be clear as to what unit you are speaking of? There's a whole section of transcript there and nobody has identified the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, we -- what we have been discussing throughout here referring to the period from the 8th of May, 1999, when Djuric [as interpreted] came to see you, we were discussing the Skorpions unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please pull up document -- Defence document D003-1945. What I would like now to be shown is page 8718, line 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, in response to a question whether you knew or had any information that some members of the Skorpions also been deployed in Bosnia, you said, No, we had no such information.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I can't speak or read English, and I don't know why you're showing me this. Could you please translate? Could you tell me what the question was?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, the question was whether you knew or had any information that the Skorpions had also been deployed in Bosnia, or engaged in Bosnia, you said, No, we did not have that information.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is probably a reference to my service up until the 8th of May, 1992, and up until that period, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, when did the operations in Bosnia start?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we consider them to have begun in early May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. So that's when the operations began?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had no information that the Skorpions had been deployed in Bosnia. Up until then they hadn't. And at that point, I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But here the question is about some information. When did you get some information about their engagement in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I read about it in the Vreme Weekly while I was still retired, and this was an article about the paramilitary unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, and based on the information that you received from the counter-intelligence group, do you know that among the members of that unit, which had been disbanded in 1996, 20 to 30 members of that old unit had been sent to Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no such information as to the new and old membership of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that an on-site investigation was conducted in Podujevo immediately following the incident? In other words, as early as the 30th of March and that this investigation was done by an investigating judge of the district court?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you what I learned subsequently. I can't tell you anything about what I knew at the time. What I learned was that those bodies had been there for three days on a pile in the yard because allegedly the investigating judge wasn't able to come to the site because of the roads. The situation on the roads. This is what I've learned from -- after reading the documents from the proceedings, the court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that an investigating -- investigation was conducted?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, after three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a criminal complaint was submitted and that some individuals were indicted?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, but I know that the trace evidence was not fixated on the spot. It wasn't established exactly who had opened fire, who had killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: Once a criminal complaint is submitted and when an investigation is initiated, can the investigating judge -- can any -- can the police have any influence on the further proceedings?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in some cases, yes, if they find or learn any new information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And once the court determines that some individuals should be remanded in custody, then that is the sole decision of the court?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the sole decision of the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In that phase of the proceedings; correct? I need to repeat my question because I believe that the -- that your answer was not recorded fully. My question was: When the police submits a criminal report and once an investigation is initiated, am I correct that they can no longer have any say in the further proceedings? Could you please answer.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that they could not influence the further proceedings. However, if they found any new information in the course of their operative work, then they could submit that information to the Prosecutor or the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I would now like to move on to the meeting held on the 17th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Exhibit D003-2495 on the screens. Paragraph 64. This should be page 16 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you please read paragraph 64, General.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you keep asking me to read things and at one point I was told that I wasn't just a puppet reading things, but okay let me read it. It says here: "The minister of Internal Affairs, Vlajko Stojiljkovic, was not present. His absence was strange and was not explained. There were five generals from the Army of Yugoslavia and not a single general from the police in command of forces in Kosovo. Holding such a meeting was a normal thing, but not everybody best versed in the situation on the ground was there. Stevanovic, Lukic, and particularly Stojiljkovic should have been there as well."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Is your statement and as you recollect the events from the time, is it correctly relayed in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think, yes, more or less. Whether General Djordjevic was mentioned, I don't know. You also have a statement that is also in evidence here, notes that I took during this meeting, and that would be the most accurate information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And thereto it says that General Djordjevic was not present; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And all the information that you did receive regarding that, you received from Rade Markovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which information you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, when you said about "what he had reported?"

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he wasn't speaking to me, he was just answering Milosevic's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I was just quoting what was mentioned in your notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just now like to -- please bear with me a moment, can we pull up Exhibit P884.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are these notes already an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's Exhibit P884. I've already said that. I apologise, it would appear that my request was not entered here. Could we please see Exhibit P884. But I see now that it has been recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My question is about the document that is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the 2006/2007 statement, paragraph 64. This is the statement that the witness provided to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was only on the Defence 65 ter list to be used during the questioning of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. You are not tendering it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, I have a question for you relating to the very beginning of your notes. You said that both you and Mr. Pavkovic submitted written reports and that what you did in fact in the meeting was read them out. Now, I would like to know whether you had ever seen your written report after this briefing? And I'm referring to the proceedings before this Tribunal, not anything else.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, do you mean the report from the meeting of the 17th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to be shown the report that was submitted by Pavkovic on the 17th of May?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this now, since you had the report, the report was written if I understood you correctly, you said that there was no need for you to write the contents of this report; however, at the very beginning here, I see in paragraph 1 General Pavkovic then submitted his report and then colon and it says, There is no problem with the Petrusic group. There is an error here. Now, could you tell me what Pavkovic actually reported on when you wrote this down in your notes?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what I wrote down in my notes, I'm not sure. I just para-phrased some of his overall -- some portions ever his overall briefing. This is what I noted in my notebook, and he didn't know what it was that I wrote down. What I wrote down was just the parts that I -- the portions that I considered interest -- of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I think you misunderstood me. I believe that you said that you didn't want to make any notes on his report because the report was in written form and there was no need for it; but in addition to that and in spite of that, the first sentence of your notes here is that General Pavkovic gave his report and then: "There is no problem with the Petrusic ..." -- there is an error here, it says the "Petronijevic group." So could you tell us then, What is it that he said about this?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean what he said about the Petrusic group? Well, what he said was that they were disarmed, that they were taken in custody, that Petrusic and Orasanin were arrested, and that the entire group was disbanded, and that currently there was an operative investigation underway as to what they had committed, what acts they had committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you just one more thing: Were the proceedings against them conducted in the Pristina Corps or in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was done in Belgrade, and I can explain why this was so. The operatives from the RDB were supposed to take part in the investigation because they insisted that these were French agents. And when they were arrested, Rade Markovic was informed an operative came and said that he would bring some material the next day and then for an entire month after that there was no one from the RDB attending those proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have page K061-7039 we need the second page, second paragraph, in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just scroll this down a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at this and then further on up to there you commented the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But then if we can just get the next page in the B/C/S version but just after a moment, once the witness has been able to read this. Could we now have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a record of his notes which flows from page to page, and he can't even see a whole page here. Perhaps he could be shown the binder that he has here with his notes, and I think it's document 91 in the binder that he has. If it would be more practical for him to look at the document that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's tab 91. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you want to look at your -- the photocopy of your notes that are there, General, rather than trying to follow them on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there's no need for that, I think I can still recollect what it was about the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, what I wanted to ask you was to tell me and explain the remarks here by Mr. Milosevic. So you commented the questions of the Prosecution up to there and then we stopped there. You didn't comment anything on Milosevic's words at that meeting, so now I would like to ask you to tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after it was determined that the Petrusic group had been resolved or dissolved, that Petrusic had been arrested, Milosevic said that we should be careful lest someone else was infiltrated, the new group that we would have to deal with. And in connection with that, he demanded that additional security measures be taken on the borders with Republika Srpska because we had information that there was a group -- the Vukovi from the Drina, if I'm not mistaken that was their name. The Wolves from the Drina. And there was also a portion that I did not mention during my testimony there, because the questions -- there were no questions about it. And that was this: Both General Pavkovic and General Ojdanic, and Vice-President Sainovic agreed with them, they all ask that a special state commission be established in Belgrade which would go to Kosovo and investigate the events mentioned and discussed in the meeting. And what struck me, and I testified about this earlier, and once we went out of the meeting I told my colleagues that this was really unusual that a -- that this topic of creating a special committee for Kosovo was completely obviated, and that's why we came to the meeting. Following this, President Milosevic put the stress on the need for us to meet regularly because apparently there was not proper or sufficient communication and cooperation between the RDB and the military services. Partly for that reason but especially because of what General Pavkovic said and that was the refusal to create a Joint Commission to investigate those 597 bodies where it was necessary to establish in whose area of responsibility they had been found. And then he also had an objection regarding a recent statement by the spokesman. This was a TV appearance where the MUP claimed that these were only small groups of individuals and that those groups had already been dealt with. And in that sense, he remarked that one should be careful lest NATO concluded that they must come to Kosovo to deal with these groups. Well, in brief, this is what it was, I can tell you a bit more but.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me that last paragraph in your report that Jugoslav Petrusic, on the basis of the -- it says VK positions here was held in custody for three days?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I've been saying. I took him into custody, him and Orasanin too, and I had the authority to do that pursuant to the law on holding people into custody up to 72 hours in emergency situations; however, in war this was extended to a period of 30 days.
